summary: Provides guidelines for registering and administering internationalized domain names in Chinese, Japanese and Korean. It deals with the problem of characters that look alike, and with deployment and administration issues beyond the IDNA protocol itself. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3743 gives registries a way to check CJK domain labels and group similar spellings under one holder. Each zone chooses the tables that define valid characters and their variants.

subtitle: Guidelines for registering CJK domain labels and handling similar character variants.

tldr.problem: Chinese, Japanese, and Korean labels can use different code points for related or similar-looking characters, which can confuse users and create opportunities for fraud.
tldr.mechanism: A zone uses a Language Variant Table for each language to validate characters and generate preferred and character-variant labels. The labels are grouped into one IDL Package for a holder.
tldr.outcome: Preferred variants are normally activated, while other character variants are reserved. The protection depends on each zone's tables and policies; the memo is Informational guidance.

today: RFC 3743 is an Informational document from April 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides guidelines that zone administrators may apply according to local policy.

sections.title: Why CJK Domain Labels Need Guidelines
sections.content:
Domain names were designed as identifiers without language context, but users increasingly read them as words and names. In Chinese, Japanese, and Korean (CJK), one conceptual character can be represented by different code points, increasing the chance of confusion.

IDNA and its supporting specifications handle string preparation and encoding. This memo addresses administrative practices for zones: how they can define valid characters and manage similar variants during registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Similar-looking CJK characters can create domain labels that users mistake for one another. These guidelines describe how a zone can group such labels during registration.

sections.title: Language Variant Tables and IDL Packages
sections.content:
A zone uses a Language Variant Table for each language it permits. Each table has three columns: Valid Code Point, Preferred Variant, and Character Variant. The first lists characters allowed in that language; the others list possible substitutions.

Preferred variants are normally activated in the zone file. Other character variants are usually reserved without being activated. The original label and its language associations, active variants, and reserved variants form one IDL Package, treated as an atomic unit.
sections.plainLanguage: For each language, a table lists allowed characters and possible variants. The registry groups the original label and its variants into one package for a single holder.

sections.title: Principles for Registration
sections.content:
The guidelines recommend associating each Internationalized Domain Label (IDL) with one or more languages and checking every character against each language's valid-code-point list. If a character is invalid for an associated language, the label is not valid for registration.

Labels generated from preferred variants should be resolvable. Labels generated from character variants should be reserved so other holders cannot register them. Zones may set additional policies to limit how many variants they reserve or activate.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry checks every character against the selected language tables. It normally activates preferred spellings and reserves other listed variants for the same holder.

sections.title: Registration and Variant Generation
sections.content:
Registration begins by processing the proposed label with Nameprep and checking whether it is available. The registry then validates it for each associated language and generates labels by substituting preferred and character variants from each table.

The original label and preferred variants form the initial set of Zone Variants, which are activated in the zone file after conversion with ToASCII. Character Variant Labels not already in that set are reserved. If two characters have three and two preferred variants, the memo says the combination process can produce 12 variant labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry processes and checks the requested label, then generates its listed variants. Preferred forms are normally activated, and other variants are reserved in the package.

sections.title: Examples from the Memo
sections.content:
The RFC gives example tables for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean languages and works through sample registrations. It warns that the example tables are incomplete and are not suitable for actual use.

In one example, a label valid for Chinese and Japanese is invalid when Korean is also selected because one code point is not valid in the Korean table. Another example produces two active zone variants when Chinese language tables prefer different spellings.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show that a label can fail if one selected language does not allow a character. Different preferred spellings can become separate active labels in the same package.

sections.title: Security and Table Quality
sections.content:
The memo says unrestricted use of non-ASCII characters can confuse users and invite attacks. Grouping similar variants under one holder and rejecting inappropriate characters can reduce some of these risks.

The protection depends on the per-zone and per-language tables. Errors in a table can significantly reduce the protection, and each zone's choices reflect its balance between risk and registration flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The guidelines can reduce some look-alike risks by reserving variants for one holder. Incorrect or incomplete tables can weaken that protection.
